overview.title: Contents (continued): chapters 5-8
overview.main_topic: Contents entries for section 5.4, chapter 6 (the universal workflow of machine learning), chapter 7 (a deep dive on Keras) and the start of chapter 8 (image classification).
overview.central_idea: The book closes its foundations with generalization techniques and an end-to-end ML workflow, deepens Keras (model-building styles, callbacks, custom training loops), and then begins its applied computer-vision chapters with ConvNets.
overview.importance: Chapters 6 and 7 are the practical toolkit used in every later chapter: how to approach a new problem, and how to build and train models flexibly in Keras.
learning_objectives: Find the generalization techniques (data curation, feature engineering, early stopping, regularization).
Identify the three phases of the universal ML workflow: define the task, develop a model, deploy it.
Locate the three ways to build Keras models and the material on callbacks, TensorBoard and custom training loops.
Find where convolution and max-pooling are introduced.

summary:
This contents page (printed ix in the header) covers four chapters.

**Section 5.4, Improving generalization (printed 158, PDF p.182)** finishes chapter 5 with dataset curation, feature engineering, early stopping and regularizing your model.

**Chapter 6, The universal workflow of machine learning (printed 171, PDF p.195)** is organized as three phases:
1. *Defining the task* — framing the problem, collecting a dataset, understanding your data, choosing a measure of success;
2. *Developing a model* — preparing data, choosing an evaluation protocol, beating a baseline, scaling up to a model that overfits, then regularizing and tuning;
3. *Deploying your model* — explaining your work and setting expectations with stakeholders, shipping an inference model, monitoring it in the wild, and maintaining it.

**Chapter 7, A deep dive on Keras (printed 190, PDF p.214)** presents a spectrum of workflows (7.1); the three ways to build models — Sequential, Functional API, and subclassing `Model` — plus mixing them and choosing the right tool (7.2); built-in training and evaluation loops with custom metrics, callbacks and TensorBoard (7.3); and writing your own training and evaluation loops, including custom training-step functions, low-level metrics, using `fit()` with a custom loop, and handling metrics in a custom `train_step()` (7.4).

**Chapter 8, Image classification (printed 231, PDF p.255)** begins with 8.1, an introduction to ConvNets: the convolution operation and the max-pooling operation. It continues on the next contents page.

deeper.title: Using printed vs. PDF page numbers
deeper.body: The numbers in this table of contents are the book's printed page numbers. This companion links by PDF page number. For the main body of the book, **PDF page = printed page + 24** (for example, chapter 6 starts on printed page 171, which is PDF p.195; chapter 8 on printed 231, PDF p.255). The offset was checked against the chapter-opener pages; it is a property of this PDF, not something the book states.

misconceptions.claim: The page numbers in the contents are the PDF page numbers.
misconceptions.correction: They are printed page numbers. In this PDF the main body is offset by 24 pages (e.g. printed 16 = PDF p.40).

takeaways: Chapter 6's workflow has three phases: define the task, develop a model, deploy it.
In development, the book's order is baseline → overfit → regularize and tune.
Chapter 7 covers three ways to build Keras models and two levels of training customization (callbacks/metrics vs. custom loops).

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as a way to build Keras models in section 7.2?
questions.explanation: Custom callbacks belong to 7.3 (built-in training loops). The other three are the model-building styles of 7.2.

questions.question: What are the three phases of the universal ML workflow in chapter 6?
questions.answer: Defining the task, developing a model, and deploying the model.

questions.question: Why does the workflow include 'Scaling up: Developing a model that overfits' before regularizing?
questions.answer: Overfitting demonstrates the model has enough capacity to learn the data; only then does it make sense to constrain it to generalize better.
questions.explanation: Inference from the subsection order in 6.2, consistent with 5.3 (improving fit) preceding 5.4 (improving generalization).
